q: A landlord in Albany charges rental applicants a $50 application fee. The actual cost of the credit and background check is $35. What is the most the landlord may lawfully charge?
explanation: RPL § 238-a caps the combined background/credit check charge at the actual cost or $20, whichever is less. The lesser of $35 and $20 is $20; no separate application or processing fee is allowed.

q: A rental applicant gives the landlord a credit and background check report obtained three weeks ago. What must the landlord do about the background-check fee?
options: Waive the fee, because the applicant supplied a report from within the past 30 days
Charge the $20 fee anyway, since the landlord may always require and bill for its own report
Charge half the usual fee for verifying the applicant's report
Charge actual cost up to $50 for a fresh report
explanation: Under RPL § 238-a, the landlord must waive the fee when the applicant provides a background or credit check conducted within the past 30 days. Three weeks falls inside that window.

q: A landlord of an ordinary (non-regulated) apartment renting for $2,600 per month asks the new tenant for first month's rent, last month's rent, and a two-month security deposit at lease signing. What is the most the landlord may collect at signing?
explanation: GOL § 7-108 caps any deposit or advance at one month's rent, and a 'last month's rent' advance counts toward that cap. The landlord may collect first month's rent ($2,600) plus a deposit/advance of $2,600, for $5,200 total.

q: After a tenant of an ordinary residential rental moves out, how long does the landlord have to return the security deposit with an itemized statement of any deductions?
options: 30 days
10 business days
14 days
60 days
explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires the landlord to provide an itemized statement and return any remaining deposit within 14 days after the tenant vacates. Missing the deadline forfeits the landlord's right to retain any portion.

q: Which statement correctly describes a New York tenant's pre-move-out inspection right for an ordinary residential rental?
options: The landlord inspects only after the tenant returns the keys, and no advance notice to the tenant is required
The landlord must inspect monthly during the final 90 days of the lease, on 24 hours' oral notice to the tenant each time
Inspection is required only at move-in; any later damage is settled from the deposit after the tenant leaves
On the tenant's request, inspect 1 to 2 weeks before move-out on 48 hours' written notice so the tenant can cure issues
explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires the landlord to tell the tenant of the right to request an inspection no earlier than two weeks and no later than one week before the tenancy ends, on at least 48 hours' written notice. The tenant may then cure the noted conditions before vacating.

q: A tenant's monthly rent is $1,400. Rent due on the 1st is paid on the 9th. What is the maximum late fee the landlord may charge?
explanation: RPL § 238-a limits late fees to $50 or 5% of monthly rent, whichever is less. 5% × $1,400 = $70, so the $50 cap controls. Payment more than five days late allows a fee.

q: A tenant's $900 rent is due on the 1st and is paid on the 4th. The lease provides a late fee. What may the landlord charge?
options: $45, which is 5% of the monthly rent and less than the $50 statutory cap
No late fee, because the rent was paid within five days of the due date
$50, the statutory maximum, because the lease expressly provides a late fee
$9 per day for each day late, as long as the total stays under $50
explanation: Under RPL § 238-a, no late fee may be charged unless rent remains unpaid more than five days after it was due. Paid on the 4th, the rent is within the grace period, so no fee is allowed even though the lease provides one.

q: A landlord of an ordinary rental tells an approved applicant to pay a $300 non-refundable 'move-in processing fee' in addition to first month's rent and a one-month security deposit. Is this lawful?
options: Yes, as long as the fee is disclosed in writing in the lease and on the rental application
Yes, because a processing fee under 15% of one month's rent is allowed for approved applicants
No; aside from the capped background/credit check fee, no fee may be charged before or at lease start
No, but only because the fee is non-refundable; a refundable processing fee of that amount would be allowed
explanation: RPL § 238-a bars landlords from demanding any payment, fee, or charge for processing an application or before or at the beginning of a tenancy, other than the capped background/credit check fee. Labeling it refundable would not make an extra deposit lawful, because GOL § 7-108 caps deposits at one month.

q: A New York City landlord hires a broker to list and fill a vacant apartment. Under the FARE Act, who pays that broker's fee?
options: The tenant, as long as the fee is clearly disclosed in the listing
The tenant and landlord split it equally
The tenant, unless the monthly rent exceeds a set luxury threshold
The landlord; the tenant cannot be charged for the landlord's agent
explanation: The NYC FARE Act (effective June 11, 2025) bars charging a tenant the fee of a broker who represents or was engaged by the landlord. Disclosure does not shift the fee to the tenant.
citation: NYC FARE Act (Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses Act), eff. June 11, 2025

q: In New York City, a tenant voluntarily signs an agreement hiring her own broker to find an apartment, agreeing to a fee of 12% of the first year's rent. She leases a unit at $3,000 per month. What is the result?
options: She may pay her own broker $4,320
The fee is prohibited by the FARE Act, so she owes nothing
She owes $360, since fees are based on one month's rent
The landlord must pay her broker $4,320
explanation: The FARE Act stops tenants from paying the landlord's agent, but a tenant may still hire and pay her own broker. $3,000 × 12 = $36,000 annual rent; $36,000 × 12% = $4,320.

q: A salesperson is showing an apartment in a three-family house to a prospective tenant on behalf of the landlord. Which agency disclosure form must the salesperson provide?
options: DOS-1736, the New York State Disclosure Form for Buyer and Seller
DOS-1735, the New York State Disclosure Form for Landlord and Tenant
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
The FARE Act fee disclosure, which replaces the agency form
explanation: For rentals of 1-4 family residential property (and condo/co-op units), RPL § 443 requires the Landlord and Tenant disclosure form, DOS-1735. DOS-1736 is the buyer/seller version used for sales.

q: What is the key difference between an assignment of a lease and a sublease?
options: A sublease transfers the entire remaining term; an assignment transfers only part
An assignment requires no landlord involvement; a sublease always requires a new lease
In an assignment the tenant transfers the entire remaining interest; in a sublease the tenant transfers less and keeps an interest
An assignment ends the original tenant's liability automatically; a sublease creates a new landlord-tenant relationship with the owner
explanation: An assignment transfers the tenant's whole remaining leasehold, while a sublease transfers part of it and the original tenant keeps an interest. Neither one automatically releases the original tenant from contractual liability to the landlord.

q: A tenant in a 12-unit privately owned building (not rent-regulated) asks the landlord in writing for consent to sublet for six months. Under RPL § 226-b, how may the landlord respond?
options: Refuse for any reason or no reason, since the lease bars subletting
Ignore the request, since only rent-stabilized tenants may sublet
Charge a sublet fee equal to one month's rent before considering it
Withhold consent only on reasonable grounds
explanation: In buildings with four or more residential units, RPL § 226-b lets a tenant sublet with the landlord's written consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld. The tenant must follow the statute's written request procedure.

q: A lease clause says the tenant waives all warranty of habitability claims in exchange for a $100-per-month rent reduction. What is the effect of the clause?
options: It is void; the warranty of habitability cannot be waived
It is enforceable because the tenant received consideration
It is enforceable only for leases longer than one year
It is valid unless the landlord fails to make repairs within 30 days
explanation: RPL § 235-b implies a warranty of habitability in every residential lease, and any agreement waiving it is void as against public policy. Consideration does not save the waiver.

q: A tenant is two months behind on rent. While the tenant is at work, the landlord changes the locks and puts the tenant's belongings in storage. What is the best description of the landlord's action?
options: Lawful, because two months of unpaid rent allows a residential landlord to retake possession of the apartment
An unlawful eviction; the landlord must go to court, and only a marshal or sheriff may execute a warrant
Lawful, as long as the landlord first served a 14-day written rent demand and waited it out
Lawful, because the tenant's belongings were safely stored rather than thrown away
explanation: New York prohibits residential self-help eviction. Removing a tenant by changing locks or removing possessions without a court order is unlawful eviction under RPAPL § 768; only a court-issued warrant executed by a marshal or sheriff can remove the tenant.

q: In a New York City multiple dwelling, a landlord must install window guards in an apartment where a child of what age lives (or where the tenant requests them)?
options: Under 6
Under 18
10 years old or younger
12 years old or younger
explanation: The NYC Health Code requires window guards in apartments where a child 10 or younger resides, and in any apartment whose tenant requests them. 'Under 6' is the threshold for the separate NYC lead paint rule.

q: Under New York City's lead paint law, the landlord's annual notice asks tenants in older buildings whether a child of what age lives in the apartment?
options: 10 years old or younger
Under 18
Under 12
Under 6
explanation: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 targets children under 6, who are most vulnerable to lead poisoning; landlords must ask annually and perform required inspections and work where such a child resides. The 10-or-younger age belongs to the window guard rule.
citation: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 (Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Act)

q: For a rent-stabilized apartment in New York City, who sets the maximum allowable rent increase for a renewal lease?
options: The NYC Rent Guidelines Board
The building owner, based on market rents
The NYS Department of State
The New York Attorney General
explanation: The Rent Guidelines Board votes each year on the maximum increases for one- and two-year renewal leases of rent-stabilized units, and the tenant chooses the term. NYS Homes and Community Renewal administers the program; DOS and the AG do not set rents.
citation: NYC Rent Stabilization Law (NYC Admin Code Title 26, Chapter 4)

q: A buyer's offer on a house has just been accepted, and the office manager asks the salesperson for the deal sheet. Which set of information is essential to include?
options: The MLS photos, listing remarks, number of showings, and feedback from every buyer who toured the home
The buyer's age, marital status, number of children, and place of employment for the seller's review
Price, deposit, mortgage amount, contingencies, closing date, broker compensation split, and both attorneys' contacts
Only the accepted price and the parties' names, since the attorneys will gather and negotiate every other term themselves
explanation: The deal sheet (memorandum of sale) summarizes the accepted terms so the attorneys can draft the contract: price, earnest money, financing, contingencies, closing date, listing/cooperating broker compensation, and contact details for both attorneys. Protected-class details are irrelevant and should not be recorded.
citation: NY brokerage practice (memorandum of sale / deal sheet)

q: A deal sheet shows an accepted price of $640,000, a mortgage of 80% of the price, and a 10% contract deposit. Excluding closing costs, what are the mortgage amount and the remaining down payment due at closing?
options: Mortgage $576,000; $64,000 due at closing
Mortgage $512,000; $128,000 due at closing
Mortgage $448,000; $64,000 due at closing
Mortgage $512,000; $64,000 due at closing
explanation: Mortgage = $640,000 × 0.80 = $512,000, so the down payment is $640,000 - $512,000 = $128,000. The deposit of $640,000 × 0.10 = $64,000 counts toward the down payment, leaving $128,000 - $64,000 = $64,000 due at closing.
citation: Real estate math (loan amount and down payment)

q: On a $640,000 sale, the listing agreement provides a 5% commission, split 60% to the listing broker and 40% to the cooperating (selling) broker. How much does the cooperating broker receive?
explanation: Total commission = $640,000 × 0.05 = $32,000. Cooperating broker's share = $32,000 × 0.40 = $12,800; the listing broker receives $32,000 × 0.60 = $19,200.

q: After an accepted offer, the buyer asks whether the signed deal sheet means the seller can no longer accept another buyer. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; the deal sheet becomes the binding contract of sale as soon as the office manager signs it
No; it summarizes terms for the attorneys, and the parties generally are not bound until both sign a contract
Yes, but only after the buyer's earnest money has been deposited in the listing broker's escrow account
No, because real estate offers in New York become binding only when they are made and accepted orally
explanation: In New York practice, the deal sheet is not the contract; the attorneys draft a contract of sale, and the deal is generally not binding until both parties sign it (the statute of frauds requires a signed writing for real property sales). Until then, the seller may still entertain other offers.

q: A tenant of an ordinary market-rate apartment in Buffalo moved out on March 1. The landlord, who wants to deduct for a window the tenant broke, does not send an itemized statement until March 25. What is the result under the security-deposit law?
options: The landlord forfeits the right to keep any part of the deposit
The landlord may still deduct, since the tenant caused the damage
The landlord must add a late charge of 5% to the refund owed
The landlord may keep the deposit but must pay the tenant interest
explanation: The landlord must return the deposit with an itemized statement of deductions within 14 days after the tenant vacates; missing that deadline forfeits the right to retain any portion. Tenant-caused damage is normally deductible, but only if it is itemized on time.

q: After a three-year tenancy, a landlord lists several charges against the tenant's security deposit. Which one is a proper deduction?
options: Repainting walls that faded from normal living
Replacing carpet worn thin along the hallway path
Replacing a door the tenant's dog chewed through
Fixing damage left by the previous tenant
explanation: Deductions are limited to items such as unpaid rent or utilities and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. Faded paint and carpet worn by normal use are ordinary wear, and a prior occupant's damage cannot be charged to this tenant.

q: A landlord of a 20-unit building holds a tenant's $3,000 security deposit in an interest-bearing New York bank account that earned 2% this year. If the landlord takes the maximum administrative fee allowed, how much of the year's interest belongs to the tenant?
explanation: Buildings with six or more units must hold deposits in interest-bearing accounts; the landlord may keep 1% per year of the deposit as an administrative fee. Interest: $3,000 × 2% = $60; fee: $3,000 × 1% = $30; tenant: $60 − $30 = $30. The $59.40 trap takes 1% of the interest instead of 1% of the deposit.

q: A tenant's $850 monthly rent is due on the 1st and is paid on the 10th. The lease provides for a late fee. What is the most the landlord may charge?
explanation: Rent paid more than five days late may draw a late fee capped at the lesser of $50 or 5% of monthly rent: $850 × 5% = $42.50, which is less than $50. The $50 figure is the ceiling only when 5% of the rent exceeds $50 (rent above $1,000).

q: Rent due on the 1st still has not arrived on the 7th. What written step does New York law require the landlord to take at this point?
options: Serve a three-day notice to pay the rent or move out
Post a notice of default on the door of the apartment
Mail the tenant a notice of nonpayment by certified mail
Wait 30 days before contacting the tenant about rent
explanation: If rent is not received within five days of the due date, the landlord must send a written notice of nonpayment by certified mail; failing to do so is an affirmative defense in a nonpayment case. The three-day demand is the pre-2019 rule, now replaced by a 14-day rent demand.

q: A landlord's screening policy rejects any applicant who appears in a housing-court database as a party to a past landlord-tenant case, even a case the tenant won. Is the policy lawful in New York?
options: No; refusing to rent because of a past landlord-tenant case is prohibited
Yes, provided the policy is applied equally to every applicant
Yes, because housing-court records are public information
Yes, but only for prior cases that ended in a money judgment
explanation: Since 2019, New York bars landlords from refusing to rent to an applicant because of the applicant's involvement in a prior landlord-tenant action or summary proceeding (the so-called tenant blacklist ban). Applying an unlawful policy uniformly does not make it lawful.

q: A Rochester landlord does not plan to renew the lease of a tenant who has lived in the apartment for 18 months. How much advance written notice must the landlord give?
options: 30 days
90 days
14 days
60 days
explanation: Notice of nonrenewal (or of a rent increase of 5% or more) depends on the longer of occupancy or lease term: under 1 year, 30 days; at least 1 but under 2 years, 60 days; 2 years or more, 90 days. Eighteen months falls in the 60-day tier.

q: A tenant has occupied an apartment for three years. At renewal the landlord wants to raise the rent by 7%. What notice is required?
options: At least 60 days' written notice of the increase
At least 90 days' written notice of the increase
At least 30 days' written notice of the increase
No notice, because the increase is under 10%
explanation: An increase of 5% or more triggers advance written notice, and a tenancy of two years or longer requires 90 days. The 10% distractor confuses this rule with the Good Cause presumptive-unreasonableness cap.

q: A landlord plans to renew a two-year tenant's lease with a 4% rent increase. The unit is not rent-regulated and not covered by Good Cause Eviction. Does the advance-notice statute require notice of this increase?
options: No; for a renewal increase, notice applies only at 5% or more
Yes; 90 days' notice applies to any rent increase at all
Yes; 30 days' notice applies to any rent increase at all
No; the notice rule applies only to lease non-renewals
explanation: Section 226-c requires advance notice only for nonrenewal or a rent increase of 5% or more; a 4% increase falls below the trigger. The trap that the rule covers only non-renewals ignores the 5%-increase trigger.

q: A landlord gives a tenant of four years only 40 days' written notice of a 10% rent increase before the lease ends. What is the result?
options: The increase takes effect on the lease end date anyway
The notice is void and the tenant gets a new two-year lease
Old terms continue until 90 days after the notice was given
The tenant may stay rent-free until proper notice arrives
explanation: When the landlord gives late notice, the tenancy continues on the existing terms from the date actual notice was given until the full notice period (here 90 days for a tenancy of two years or more) runs. The law does not void the increase forever or excuse rent.

q: A tenant moved in under a one-year lease. The landlord decides not to renew when the lease ends. What is the minimum advance notice the landlord must give?
options: 30 days, because occupancy is still under one year
60 days, because the lease term is at least one year
90 days, because the lease runs a full year
None, because the lease simply expires on its own
explanation: The notice tier uses occupancy or lease term, whichever qualifies for the longer period; a lease of at least one year but under two requires 60 days even though the tenant has lived there less than a year. The 30-day tier applies only when both occupancy and lease term are under a year.

q: In February a tenant in a 20-unit apartment building files a good-faith complaint with the city code-enforcement office about a broken boiler. In September of the same year the landlord notifies the tenant that the lease will not be renewed. How is the nonrenewal treated?
options: It is lawful, because more than six months passed since the complaint
It is automatically void, and no landlord evidence can rebut it
It is lawful, because a nonrenewal is never treated as retaliation
It is presumed retaliatory, and the landlord must rebut that presumption
explanation: Since 2019, a landlord's notice to quit, eviction filing, or substantial change in tenancy terms within one year after a tenant's good-faith complaint is presumed retaliatory; the presumption is rebuttable. The six-month window was the pre-2019 rule.

q: Which tenant activity is protected from landlord retaliation?
options: Subletting without asking for the landlord's consent
Keeping a pet that the lease expressly prohibits
Organizing a tenants' association in the building
Refusing the landlord access for a scheduled repair
explanation: The retaliation statute protects good-faith complaints to government agencies, good-faith efforts to enforce lease or habitability rights, and participation in a tenants' organization. Breaking lease terms or blocking repairs is not protected activity.

q: A tenant falls asleep with the bathtub running, and the overflow ruins the bathroom floor. The tenant then withholds rent, claiming breach of the warranty of habitability. What is the best analysis?
options: The warranty does not cover a condition the tenant's own conduct caused
The landlord is strictly liable for every condition in the unit
The claim succeeds because the warranty can never be limited
The claim succeeds only if the lease expressly mentions the warranty
explanation: The warranty of habitability is implied and cannot be waived, but the landlord is not liable for conditions caused by the misconduct of the tenant or persons under the tenant's control. 'Non-waivable' does not mean the landlord insures against the tenant's own acts.

q: Which statement accurately describes New York's warranty of habitability?
options: It applies only to written leases that expressly recite it
It covers the apartment itself but never lobbies or hallways
It applies only in buildings containing three or more units
It is implied in every residential lease and covers common areas
explanation: The warranty is implied in every residential lease, written or oral, and covers the premises and areas used in connection with them; the landlord warrants they are fit for habitation and free of conditions dangerous to life, health, or safety.

q: A tenant in a 30-unit building mails a complete sublet request to the landlord by certified mail. The landlord never responds. What is the effect after 30 days?
options: The request is deemed denied and the tenant may not sublet
The landlord's silence is deemed consent to the sublet
The tenant is released from the lease on 30 days' notice
The tenant must refile the request before any sublet
explanation: The landlord must respond within 30 days after the request (or any requested additional information) is mailed; failure to respond is deemed consent. Release on 30 days' notice is the remedy for an unreasonably refused assignment, not for a sublet request.

q: A tenant in a privately owned three-unit building wants to sublet for the summer, but the lease prohibits subletting. Does the statutory sublet right let the tenant sublet over the landlord's objection?
options: No; the sublet right covers buildings with four or more units
Yes; consent can never be unreasonably withheld in any building
Yes; any lease clause barring sublets is void as a matter of law
No; the sublet right covers only rent-stabilized apartments
explanation: The statutory right to sublet with consent that may not be unreasonably withheld applies to tenants in dwellings with four or more residential units; in a three-unit building the lease terms control. The right is not limited to rent-stabilized units.

q: A tenant asks the landlord to consent to assigning the lease to a creditworthy friend. The landlord refuses without giving any reason. If the refusal is unreasonable, what is the tenant's remedy?
options: An automatic right to complete the assignment
A rent abatement for the rest of the lease term
Release from the lease on 30 days' notice
Release from the lease on 90 days' notice
explanation: A landlord may withhold consent to an assignment, but if consent is unreasonably withheld, the tenant's sole remedy is release from the lease on request with 30 days' notice. The tenant does not gain a right to force the assignment through.

q: A rent-stabilized tenant whose legal regulated rent is $1,800 per month lawfully sublets the apartment fully furnished. What is the most the tenant may charge the subtenant?
explanation: A stabilized prime tenant may charge a subtenant the legal regulated rent plus a surcharge of up to 10% if the unit is sublet fully furnished: $1,800 × 1.10 = $1,980. The $2,160 trap applies 20%, and $1,800 ignores the furnished surcharge.

q: A lease names only one tenant. Without the landlord's consent, whom may that tenant share the apartment with?
options: Immediate family only, unless the landlord later consents in writing
Immediate family and up to two unrelated adults and their children
One other adult occupant, but none of that occupant's children
Immediate family, one other occupant, and that occupant's dependent children
explanation: Under the roommate law, a sole named tenant may share with immediate family, one additional occupant, and the occupant's dependent children, provided the tenant or spouse occupies the unit as a primary residence. A lease clause restricting occupancy further is unenforceable to that extent.

q: A tenant who lived with a lawful roommate under the roommate law moves out when the lease ends. What right does the roommate have to remain?
options: The roommate automatically becomes the tenant of record
The roommate may stay one more year at the same rent
None, unless the landlord expressly consents in writing
The roommate may stay if they paid half of the rent
explanation: An occupant added under the roommate law gains no right to continued occupancy if the tenant leaves, unless the landlord gives express written consent. Paying part of the rent does not convert the occupant into a tenant.

q: Before starting a nonpayment proceeding against a residential tenant, what written rent demand must the landlord serve?
options: A demand giving the tenant at least 14 days to pay
A demand giving the tenant at least 3 days to pay
A demand giving the tenant at least 30 days to pay
A demand giving the tenant at least 5 days to pay
explanation: Since the 2019 HSTPA, a nonpayment proceeding requires a written demand giving the tenant at least 14 days to pay (formerly 3 days). The 5-day figure is the separate certified-mail late-rent notice trigger, not the rent demand.

q: A homeowner lets a friend stay in a spare room with no lease and no rent. After seven weeks the homeowner wants the friend out and changes the locks while the friend is away. What is the best analysis?
options: Lawful, because the friend never signed a lease or paid any rent
Lawful, because self-help is allowed in an owner-occupied home
Unlawful only if the homeowner also removed the friend's belongings
Unlawful; an occupant of 30+ days can be removed only by court process
explanation: It is unlawful to evict, without a court-issued warrant executed by a marshal, sheriff, or constable, anyone who has lawfully occupied a dwelling for 30 consecutive days or longer, even without a lease. Changing the locks alone is a prohibited lockout.

q: To pressure a tenant who is behind on rent to leave, a landlord shuts off the apartment's heat and hot water. How does New York law treat this?
options: As a permitted step once a 14-day rent demand goes unpaid
As an unlawful eviction, punishable as a class A misdemeanor
As lawful if the lease lets the landlord suspend services
As a building-code violation with no eviction consequences
explanation: Interrupting or discontinuing essential services to force out an occupant is an unlawful eviction: a class A misdemeanor, plus civil penalties of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation. A rent demand starts court process; it never authorizes self-help.

q: A New York City apartment covered by the Good Cause Eviction Law rents for $2,400 per month. Assume the applicable annual CPI change is 3%. Above what monthly renewal rent is an increase presumptively unreasonable?
explanation: The threshold is the lower of 5% plus CPI or 10%. Here 5% + 3% = 8%, which is lower than 10%: $2,400 × 1.08 = $2,592. The $2,640 trap applies 10% without comparing; $2,520 uses 5% alone.

q: Under the Good Cause Eviction Law, which reason, standing alone, is NOT good cause for a covered landlord to refuse to renew a tenant?
options: The tenant has failed to pay the rent owed
The tenant is using the unit for an illegal purpose
The lease term has simply come to its end
The tenant unreasonably refused access for repairs
explanation: For covered units, expiration of the lease alone is not grounds to refuse renewal. Nonpayment, illegal use, and unreasonable refusal of access for required repairs are among the listed good-cause grounds.

q: Four New York City apartments each rent for well below any high-rent exemption level. Which one is exempt from the Good Cause Eviction Law?
options: A market-rate unit in a 40-unit building built in 1965
A rent-stabilized unit in a 1960s elevator building
A market-rate unit owned by a landlord with 60 units
A market-rate unit in a prewar walk-up with 12 units
explanation: Good Cause exempts units already governed by rent regulation, such as rent stabilization, which has its own renewal and rent rules. Older market-rate units owned by landlords above the small-landlord threshold are covered.

q: A New York City rental building received its first certificate of occupancy in 2015. Its market-rate units are owned by a large landlord. How does the Good Cause Eviction Law apply to them?
options: They are covered, because the landlord owns more than ten units
They are covered once each tenant's first lease is renewed
They are exempt only if the building has fewer than six units
They are exempt for 30 years from the date that certificate issued
explanation: Housing whose first certificate of occupancy issued on or after January 1, 2009 is exempt from Good Cause for 30 years from issuance. Portfolio size matters only for the separate small-landlord exemption.

q: A tenant in a village outside New York City asks whether the Good Cause Eviction Law protects her apartment. What determines coverage?
options: Nothing; the law applies automatically to every rental statewide
Only whether her current lease was signed after April 2024
Whether her locality opted in, and whether the unit is exempt
Only whether her building contains six or more apartments
explanation: Good Cause applies automatically in New York City but elsewhere only in localities that opt in, and even then exemptions (small landlords, regulated units, newer buildings, high-rent units, and others) can apply. The six-unit test belongs to rent stabilization under ETPA.

q: A rent-stabilized tenant in New York City believes she is being charged more than the legal regulated rent. Which body handles her overcharge complaint?
options: NYS Division of Housing and Community Renewal
NYC Rent Guidelines Board
NYS Department of State, Licensing Services
NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
explanation: DHCR (part of NYS Homes and Community Renewal) administers rent stabilization, including rent registrations and overcharge complaints. The Rent Guidelines Board only sets the annual renewal-increase percentages; it does not decide individual complaints.
citation: Rent Stabilization Law; Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR Parts 2520–2531)

q: Which change did the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 make to rent stabilization?
options: It created a 20% vacancy bonus on each apartment turnover
It required the Legislature to renew the law every year
It exempted all buildings with fewer than 50 apartments
It ended high-rent vacancy deregulation of stabilized units
explanation: The HSTPA ended high-rent vacancy and high-income deregulation, eliminated the vacancy bonus, and made the rent laws permanent rather than subject to periodic renewal. The 20% vacancy bonus is the opposite of what the law did.
citation: Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019

q: A New York City rent-stabilized tenant's lease expires on August 31. When must the owner offer a renewal lease, and what term may the tenant choose?
options: 30 to 60 days before expiration; a 1- or 2-year term at the owner's option
90 to 150 days before expiration; a 1- or 2-year term at the tenant's option
90 to 150 days before expiration; a 2-year term only, set by the owner
60 to 90 days before expiration; a 1-year term only, set by the owner
explanation: The owner must offer renewal on the DHCR form no more than 150 and no fewer than 90 days before the lease expires, and the tenant chooses a one- or two-year term at the Rent Guidelines Board rate for that term. The tenant then has 60 days to accept.

q: In New York City, a broker posts a rental listing online with the landlord's permission. A prospective tenant contacts the broker and rents the unit. May the broker collect a fee from the tenant?
options: No; an agent listing with permission may not charge the tenant
Yes, if the tenant signs a separate fee agreement at the showing
Yes, if the fee is capped at one month's rent for the unit
No, unless the landlord refuses to pay the broker any fee
explanation: Under the FARE Act, an agent who publishes a listing with the landlord's permission may not impose or collect any fee from the tenant, and an agent who publishes a listing is rebuttably presumed to have that permission. Signing a fee agreement at the showing does not change that.
citation: NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21(a)(2), (e) (FARE Act, effective June 11, 2025)

q: A New York City listing agent tells applicants they may apply for an apartment only if they first sign an agreement making the agent a dual agent and paying a fee. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, because the dual agency arrangement is disclosed in writing
Yes, if the fee amount was stated in the listing beforehand
No; a rental cannot be conditioned on hiring any agent, dual or not
No, unless the agent holds a broker's rather than salesperson's license
explanation: The FARE Act prohibits conditioning the rental of an apartment on the tenant engaging any agent, including a dual agent. Written disclosure of dual agency does not cure the prohibited condition.

q: Compared with the sale of the same 1965-built house, what does the federal lead-based paint rule NOT require when the house is leased for one year?
options: Disclosing any known lead-based paint or lead hazards
Giving the tenant a 10-day opportunity to test for lead
Providing the EPA lead hazard information pamphlet
Including a lead warning statement in the lease
explanation: For pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, give the EPA pamphlet, and include a lead warning statement, just as sellers do. The 10-day risk-assessment or inspection opportunity applies only to purchasers.

q: NYC's lead law (Local Law 1 of 2004) presumes that paint contains lead in which apartments?
options: Any apartment in a residential building built before 1978
Units with a child under 6 in buildings of 6+ units built before 1974
Any apartment in any building where a child under 6 resides
Units with a child under 6 in buildings of 3+ units built before 1960
explanation: Local Law 1 presumes that paint is lead-based in any dwelling unit where a child under 6 resides (and in common areas) in a multiple dwelling (three or more units) built before January 1, 1960; the owner may rebut the presumption with certified testing. The 1978 date is the federal disclosure cutoff, and the six-unit/1974 test belongs to rent stabilization.

q: A New York City landlord of a six-unit building must install window guards in an apartment where a child age 10 or under lives. Which window is excluded?
options: A window in the apartment's bathroom
A window in the apartment's kitchen
A window that opens onto a fire escape
A window that faces an interior courtyard
explanation: Window guards must go on every window in the apartment, including bathroom and kitchen windows, except a window that gives access to a fire escape, which must stay clear for emergency exit.
citation: NYC Health Code § 131.15; NYC Admin. Code § 27-2043.1

q: In a New York City apartment building, who is responsible for replacing the removable battery in a working smoke detector that the owner installed?
options: The tenant, who must keep the device maintained
The owner, within 30 days of the tenant's request
The superintendent, at least once each year
The fire department, during annual inspections
explanation: In NYC the owner must install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, but the occupant must keep them in good repair, including replacing batteries. The owner replaces devices at the end of their useful life.

q: What does New York's Amanda's Law require?
options: Smoke alarms with sealed 10-year batteries in every rental unit
Annual radon testing in every rental that has a basement
CO alarms only in buildings that contain three or more units
CO alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage
explanation: Amanda's Law (2010) extended carbon monoxide alarm requirements to one- and two-family homes and other residences that have fuel-burning appliances or systems or an attached garage, not only to larger buildings.

q: A salesperson represents a landlord who is renting out a two-family house. When must the salesperson give a prospective tenant the DOS-1735 agency disclosure?
options: At the first substantive contact with the prospective tenant
When the tenant submits a completed rental application
At lease signing, together with the lease and riders
Only if the tenant asks whom the salesperson represents
explanation: The agency disclosure is due at the first substantive contact, before the tenant shares information or negotiates. Waiting until the application or the lease signing defeats its purpose, which is to let the tenant know whose interests the agent represents before anything is said.
citation: RPL § 443; DOS-1735 (New York State Disclosure Form for Landlord and Tenant)

q: After a showing, a prospective tenant signs the DOS-1735 the landlord's salesperson gives her. She then asks whether she is now committed to renting through that firm. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; it commits her to rent through the firm for 30 days
No; her signature only acknowledges that she received the form
Yes; signing it creates a tenant's-agency relationship by law
No; it binds her only once the landlord also signs the form
explanation: The form is headed "THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT." Signing only acknowledges receipt of the agency disclosure. It does not create an agency relationship or a duty to rent, and adding the landlord's signature would not change that.

q: A prospective tenant reads the DOS-1735 the landlord's salesperson presents but refuses to sign the acknowledgment. What should the salesperson do?
options: Refuse to keep working with the tenant until the form is signed
Write 'refused' on the form and discard it after the showing
Prepare a sworn written declaration of the facts and keep it
Have the landlord sign the form in the tenant's place instead
explanation: When a consumer refuses to sign, the licensee makes a written declaration of the facts of the refusal under oath or affirmation and keeps it for at least three years. A refusal does not cancel the duty to disclose, and it does not require the agent to stop working with the tenant.

q: A listing broker at Firm A asks a salesperson at Firm B to help find a tenant for Firm A's landlord client. The Firm B salesperson does not represent any tenant. Which relationship should the Firm B salesperson check on DOS-1735?
options: Tenant's agent for the prospective tenant
Dual agent for both the landlord and tenant
Landlord's agent engaged directly by the landlord
Broker's agent acting in the landlord's interest
explanation: A broker's agent is engaged by the listing agent, works at a different firm, and has no direct relationship with the landlord. The listing agent directs that work and answers for it, and the landlord has no vicarious liability for the broker's agent. That lack of a direct engagement is what separates it from a landlord's agent.

q: Under New York City's FARE Act, what must every residential rental listing or advertisement disclose clearly and conspicuously?
options: The listing broker's commission split with cooperating firms
The landlord's minimum income requirement for applicants
Every fee a tenant must pay to rent the unit
The unit's complete rent history for the past four years
explanation: The FARE Act requires listings to disclose clearly and conspicuously every fee a tenant must pay to rent the unit, so tenants are not surprised at signing. It does not require a listing to show broker splits, income criteria, or rent history.
citation: NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.22(a) (FARE Act, Local Law 119 of 2024)

q: Before a New York City tenant signs a lease, which FARE Act document must the tenant receive and sign?
options: A sworn statement that the tenant chose not to hire a broker
A DOS-1736 buyer and seller agency acknowledgment form
A landlord certificate that the unit is not rent stabilized
An itemized written disclosure of all fees the tenant must pay
explanation: Before the lease is signed, the tenant must receive and sign an itemized written disclosure of every fee owed to the landlord or to a third party at the landlord's direction. The tenant gets a copy, and the landlord or agent keeps the signed disclosure for 3 years. DOS-1736 is the sales agency form; rentals use DOS-1735.

q: A salesperson posts a New York City apartment on a rental website. When an applicant calls, she says the tenant must pay her broker fee because she never signed a written listing agreement with the landlord. Which statement is correct?
options: She is presumed to list with the landlord's OK; the fee is barred
The fee is allowed since no written listing agreement exists
The fee is allowed if it is disclosed clearly in the listing
The fee is allowed if the tenant acknowledges DOS-1735
explanation: Under the FARE Act, an agent who publishes a rental listing is rebuttably presumed to do so with the landlord's permission, and an agent who lists with the landlord's permission may not charge the tenant any fee. Permission does not require a written listing agreement, so its absence alone does not rebut the presumption. Disclosing an unlawful fee in the listing does not make it lawful, and DOS-1735 is only an agency disclosure.

q: A Buffalo landlord's rental broker asks whether the FARE Act decides who pays her fee on Buffalo apartments. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes; the FARE Act governs every rental in the state
No; the FARE Act is a New York City local law
Yes; it covers any city with 100,000+ residents
No; it covers only rent-stabilized units in NYC
explanation: The FARE Act is a New York City local law (Local Law 119 of 2024), so it does not reach a Buffalo rental. Statewide rules such as RPL § 238-a's fee limits still apply there. The FARE Act is not a statewide ban on broker fees, and within NYC it is not limited to stabilized units.
citation: NYC Local Law 119 of 2024 (FARE Act); RPL § 238-a

q: A New York City listing agent tells applicants they may tour her landlord's apartment only if they first sign a tenant-representation agreement with her firm and pay her a fee. Under the FARE Act, this practice is:
options: Prohibited; access can't be conditioned on hiring a broker
Permitted, because the tenant signs the agreement voluntarily
Permitted if the fee is capped at one month's rent
Permitted if the fee is shown in the advertisement
explanation: No person may condition the rental of an NYC apartment on the tenant engaging any agent, including a dual agent; DCWP applies this even when the broker demands to be hired before the tenant can see the unit. A listing agent is also a landlord's agent, who may not collect any fee from the tenant. A tenant may still choose to hire her own broker, but a forced agreement is not voluntary, and neither a fee cap nor ad disclosure fixes it.
citation: NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21(a), (c) (FARE Act); DCWP FARE Act FAQ

q: A New York City landlord screens applicants with the common '40 times the rent' income standard. The apartment rents for $3,250 per month. What annual income must an applicant show?
explanation: $3,250 × 40 = $130,000 of annual income. $39,000 is just one year's rent ($3,250 × 12), $97,500 uses 30×, and $156,000 uses 48×.
citation: Landlord screening practice (40× monthly rent); no statute sets this multiplier

q: An applicant earns $112,000 a year and is looking at buildings that use the 40-times-the-rent income standard. What is the highest monthly rent she qualifies for?
explanation: $112,000 ÷ 40 = $2,800 per month. $3,733 divides by 30, $9,333 divides by 12 (her monthly income, not a rent ceiling), and $2,333 divides by 48.

q: An applicant earns too little to qualify, so the building's policy calls for a guarantor earning 80 times the monthly rent. The rent is $2,900. What is the minimum annual income the guarantor needs?
explanation: $2,900 × 80 = $232,000. Landlords commonly set the guarantor multiple higher than the tenant's 40× ($116,000) because the guarantor also carries their own housing costs. $34,800 is one year's rent, and $290,000 uses 100×.
citation: Landlord screening practice (guarantor multiple set by building policy)

q: A tenant asks why so many New York City landlords demand annual income of 40 times the monthly rent. Which description of this standard is accurate?
options: A state law limiting the rent any tenant may be charged
A requirement of RPL § 238-a for every rental application
A federal HUD rule that applies to all market-rate rentals
A common landlord screening policy, not a statutory rule
explanation: 40× is a business practice landlords choose, not a legal requirement, and it is subject to fair housing limits. RPL § 238-a governs application and screening fees, not income ratios, and no HUD rule sets the 40× figure.

q: An NYC apartment rents for $2,800 a month. An applicant's housing voucher pays $2,100 of it, and she pays the rest. The landlord uses a 40-times-the-rent income test. What is the most income the landlord may lawfully require of her?
options: $0, because no income test is allowed
explanation: Under source-of-income guidance, an income test may apply only to the tenant's own share of the rent: $2,800 − $2,100 = $700, and $700 × 40 = $28,000. Applying 40× to the full rent ($112,000) discriminates against voucher holders. A ban on any income test applies only when the voucher covers 100% of the rent.
citation: NYC Admin. Code § 8-107(5); NYC Commission on Human Rights source-of-income guidance; Executive Law § 296(5)

q: A graduate student's father signs a lease guaranty for her apartment. What is the father's role?
options: A co-tenant who gains the right to occupy the apartment
A third party who promises to pay if the tenant defaults
A broker who vouches for the tenant's credit to the landlord
An escrow agent who holds the tenant's security deposit
explanation: A guarantor promises to cover the tenant's lease obligations if the tenant fails to perform. A guarantor is liable but has no right to possession. That separates a guarantor from a co-tenant, who both owes the rent and may live in the unit.
citation: General Obligations Law § 5-701 (guaranty must be in a signed writing); general contract law

q: A landlord turns down an applicant solely because a screening report shows she was named in a nonpayment case that was dismissed two years ago. This rejection is:
options: Unlawful under RPL § 227-f's ban on tenant blacklisting
Lawful, because the case appears in a public court record
Lawful, as long as the landlord refunds the screening fee
Unlawful only if the tenant prevailed in the earlier case
explanation: RPL § 227-f bars refusing to rent because an applicant was involved in a past or pending landlord-tenant proceeding, whatever the outcome. If a landlord checks court or screening-bureau records and then rejects the applicant, the rejection is presumed to rest on that record. A record being public does not make relying on it lawful.

q: In New York City, a landlord hires a broker to rent an apartment at $3,400 per month. The credit and background check actually costs $30. Under current law, what is the most the tenant can be required to pay up to and including lease signing?
explanation: $3,400 first month + $3,400 security (one-month cap) + $20 screening fee (the lesser of actual cost and $20) = $6,820. The landlord's broker fee cannot be charged to the tenant under FARE, so $12,940 (adding a 15% annual fee) is wrong. $10,220 adds a last-month advance, which the one-month deposit cap does not allow, and $6,800 leaves out the lawful $20 fee.
citation: GOL § 7-108; RPL § 238-a; NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21 (FARE Act)

q: In New York City, a tenant voluntarily hires her own broker for a fee of one month's rent. She leases a $2,750-per-month apartment with a one-month security deposit and a $20 screening fee. What is her total due at signing, including her broker's fee?
explanation: $2,750 rent + $2,750 security + $20 screening + $2,750 broker fee = $8,270. FARE allows a tenant to pay a broker she hired herself. $5,520 leaves out her broker's fee, $11,020 adds an extra month's rent, and $10,470 uses a 15%-of-annual-rent fee ($4,950) the stem doesn't give.
citation: GOL § 7-108; RPL § 238-a; NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21 (tenant-hired broker allowed)

q: A Rochester landlord rents a non-regulated apartment for $1,600 a month. The applicant's background and credit check actually cost $15. What is the most the landlord may collect from the tenant up to and including lease signing?
explanation: $1,600 first month + $1,600 security (one-month cap) + $15 screening fee = $3,215. The fee is the lesser of actual cost and $20, so $3,220 overcharges. $4,815 adds a third month, and $3,250 treats the $50 late-fee cap as an upfront fee.

q: A landlord pays the listing brokerage a fee of one month's rent on a $4,200-per-month apartment. The listing salesperson's split with her broker is 60/40 in her favor. What does the salesperson earn?
explanation: The fee is $4,200, and the salesperson gets 60%: $4,200 × 0.60 = $2,520. $1,680 is the brokerage's 40%, $2,100 assumes a 50/50 split, and $4,536 applies 60% to a 15% annual-rent fee the stem doesn't give.
citation: Commission arithmetic; RPL § 442-a (salesperson paid through the broker)

q: A New York City tenant hiring her own broker is choosing between two fee offers on a $3,100-per-month apartment: (1) one month's rent, or (2) 15% of the first year's rent. Which fee is larger, and by how much?
options: The one-month fee, by $2,635
The 15% fee, by $5,580
The two fees are exactly equal
The 15% fee, by $2,480
explanation: 15% fee: $3,100 × 12 × 0.15 = $5,580. One-month fee: $3,100. Difference: $5,580 − $3,100 = $2,480. Taking 15% of a single month ($465) gives the $2,635 error, and $5,580 is the larger fee itself, not the difference.
citation: Commission arithmetic; NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21 (tenant-hired broker)

q: A salesperson places an online rental ad that shows only her name, her cell number, and the apartment details. What is wrong with the ad?
options: Her license number and expiration date must appear
The name of her associated brokerage must appear
Nothing; a salesperson may advertise in her own name
The landlord's name and phone number must appear
explanation: An ad that names a salesperson must also include the name of the broker or brokerage she is associated with; an ad lacking it is a blind ad. (The rule also requires the broker's address or phone number and an accurate statement of her license type.) License numbers, expiration dates and the landlord's contact information are not required.

q: A brokerage keeps advertising a $2,100 one-bedroom that was rented a month ago because the ad draws calls. Callers are then steered to $2,700 units. How is this practice best described?
options: Acceptable if the ad says rents start 'from $2,100'
Allowed for up to 60 days after the unit is rented
False and misleading advertising by the licensees
A violation only if callers are in a protected class
explanation: Advertising a unit the firm knows is unavailable to lure inquiries is bait advertising, which is false and misleading and can lead to licensing discipline. No grace period applies, and the conduct is improper whoever responds. The fair housing angle is a separate question.

q: A listing for a 24-unit apartment building in Albany says "No Section 8." Which statement is correct?
options: It violates the state's lawful-source-of-income protection
It is lawful because only NYC protects voucher holders
It is lawful if the landlord's broker placed the ad
It is lawful if the rule is applied to every applicant
explanation: Since 2019, the NYS Human Rights Law has protected lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, statewide, so this ad is discriminatory. Applying the exclusion to everyone is still discrimination, and a broker who places the ad shares the liability.

q: A salesperson is the landlord's agent on a New York City rental. Which sequence meets the required disclosure timing?
options: Application and screening; DOS-1735; fee disclosure; lease signing
DOS-1735; lease signing; fee disclosure; application and screening
Fee disclosure; application and screening; lease signing; DOS-1735
DOS-1735; application and screening; fee disclosure; lease signing
explanation: The agency disclosure comes at the first substantive contact. Next come the application and screening. The FARE itemized fee disclosure must be signed before the lease is signed. Giving DOS-1735 after the application, or the fee disclosure after the lease, misses the required timing.

q: At lease signing, a tenant gives the landlord's salesperson a check payable to the brokerage for first month's rent and the security deposit, both to be passed on to the landlord. What should happen to the check?
options: The salesperson deposits it in her personal account for the landlord
The broker deposits it in a special escrow account within 3 business days
The salesperson holds it uncashed until the lease term begins
The broker deposits it in the firm's operating account for the landlord
explanation: Money held for others is trust money. The broker must deposit it in a separate special account within three business days and account for it promptly. Putting it in a personal or operating account is commingling, and holding the check indefinitely fails to protect the funds.

q: A deal sheet shows an accepted price of $1,150,000, a mortgage of $920,000, and the customary NYC 10% contract deposit. What are the loan-to-value ratio and the contract deposit?
options: 80% LTV; $115,000 deposit
80% LTV; $230,000 deposit
20% LTV; $115,000 deposit
80% LTV; $92,000 deposit
explanation: LTV = $920,000 ÷ $1,150,000 = 80%. Deposit = 10% × $1,150,000 = $115,000. $230,000 is the full 20% down payment, 20% is the equity share rather than LTV, and $92,000 takes 10% of the loan instead of the price.
citation: LTV = loan ÷ price or appraised value (lower); customary NYC contract deposit

q: A deal sheet shows an $875,000 sale with a 5% commission split 50/50 between the listing and cooperating brokerages. The buyer's salesperson works at the cooperating firm on a 60/40 split in her favor. What does she earn?
explanation: $875,000 × 5% = $43,750. The co-broke half is $43,750 × 50% = $21,875, and her share is $21,875 × 60% = $13,125. $26,250 applies 60% to the whole commission, $21,875 is her firm's entire side, and $8,750 is her broker's 40%.
citation: Commission arithmetic; listing agreement and office compensation plan

q: A $1,240,000 sale carries a 6% commission, split 50/50 with the cooperating broker. The listing salesperson's split with her own broker is 70/30 in her favor. How much does the listing brokerage keep?
explanation: $1,240,000 × 6% = $74,400. The listing side is $74,400 × 50% = $37,200. The brokerage keeps 30%: $37,200 × 0.30 = $11,160. $26,040 is the agent's 70%, $22,320 takes 30% of the whole commission, and $37,200 is the whole listing side.
citation: Commission arithmetic; listing agreement and office compensation plan

q: A cooperating brokerage was offered 2.5% of the sale price and receives a $15,000 commission check at closing. What was the sale price?
explanation: Price = $15,000 ÷ 0.025 = $600,000. $300,000 divides by 5%, a total commission the stem doesn't give. $1,200,000 halves the 2.5% again, and $750,000 divides by 2%.

q: A listing agreement pays the listing brokerage 3% and offers the buyer's brokerage 2.5% on a $720,000 sale. What does the seller pay in total commission, and what does the cooperating broker receive?
options: $39,600 total; $19,800 to the co-broke
$21,600 total; $18,000 to the co-broke
$36,000 total; $18,000 to the co-broke
$39,600 total; $18,000 to the co-broke
explanation: Total: $720,000 × 5.5% = $39,600. Co-broke share: $720,000 × 2.5% = $18,000, and the listing side gets $21,600 (3%). $19,800 wrongly splits the total 50/50, $21,600 is only the listing side, and $36,000 assumes a 5% total.

q: The buyer's side of a $560,000 sale pays 2.5%. The buyer's brokerage owes another licensed broker a 25% referral fee on its side. The buyer's salesperson is then paid 50% of what her firm keeps. What does she earn?
explanation: Side: $560,000 × 2.5% = $14,000. Referral: $14,000 × 25% = $3,500, which leaves $10,500. Her 50%: $10,500 × 0.5 = $5,250. $7,000 ignores the referral, $10,500 is the firm's net, and $3,500 is the referral fee.
citation: Commission arithmetic; RPL § 442 (fees shared only with licensed brokers)

q: In a typical New York City residential sale, who holds the buyer's contract deposit after the contract is signed?
options: The listing broker, in its operating account
The seller, who may use it for moving costs
The seller's attorney, as escrow agent
The buyer's lender, until the loan closes
explanation: In NYC practice, the seller's attorney usually holds the down payment in escrow under the contract's escrow terms until closing or a proper release. It is not the seller's money to spend, and a broker may not put trust funds in an operating account.
citation: Customary NYC contract practice; escrow terms of the contract of sale

q: A buyer's offer on a Manhattan condo has been accepted. She asks whether New York law requires her to put down a 10% contract deposit. What is the best answer?
options: No; 10% is customary, and the amount is negotiable
Yes; state law requires 10% on all home contracts
Yes; lenders require exactly 10% before a commitment
No; state law caps contract deposits at 5% of price
explanation: The 10% deposit is NYC custom, not a statute. The parties may agree to a different amount, often outside NYC, and the deal sheet simply records what was agreed. No law sets a 10% requirement or a 5% cap.
citation: Customary NYC practice; contract terms control

q: After the listing agent sends out the deal sheet in a typical New York City sale, who ordinarily prepares the first draft of the contract of sale?
options: The buyer's attorney
The seller's attorney
The listing salesperson
The buyer's mortgage lender
explanation: In NYC the seller's attorney drafts the contract from the deal sheet, and the buyer's attorney reviews it, does due diligence, and negotiates riders. The salesperson supplies the deal terms but does not draft the contract, which is legal work.
citation: Customary NYC practice; Judiciary Law § 478 (practice of law)

q: A buyer's agent fills out a deal sheet that will go to both attorneys and the listing side. In the notes, she writes that her client 'could go higher if needed.' What is the problem?
options: Nothing, because a deal sheet is only an internal record
Nothing, because the price has already been agreed to
It is a problem only if the seller signs the deal sheet
It reveals the client's confidential negotiating position
explanation: A deal sheet goes to the other side, and terms can be renegotiated later, for example after an inspection. Revealing the buyer's willingness to pay more breaches the agent's fiduciary duty of confidentiality. The deal sheet is not a private office memo.
citation: Fiduciary duty of confidentiality; RPL § 443 (buyer's agent duties)

q: A salesperson is preparing a deal sheet for an accepted offer on a co-op apartment. Which contingency is standard for a co-op purchase but not for a typical house sale?
options: Approval of the deed by the county clerk
Approval of the price by the Department of State
Approval of the purchaser by the co-op board
Approval of the sale by the seller's lender
explanation: A co-op buyer acquires shares and a proprietary lease, so the board must approve the purchaser, and the deal sheet should flag board approval. A co-op sale has no deed to record, and DOS does not approve prices.
citation: Customary co-op contract practice; co-op proprietary lease and bylaws

q: An office manager tells a salesperson to write 6% on every deal sheet because 'that's the board rate in this area.' What is the correct response?
options: Commissions are negotiable; a set area rate raises antitrust issues
6% is the maximum commission allowed under New York license law
The board rate controls unless the seller objects to it in writing
The rate is fixed each year by the Department of State's rules
explanation: Each commission is negotiated between the broker and the client. Brokers who agree on or enforce a standard area rate risk price-fixing liability under antitrust law. Neither DOS nor license law sets or caps commission rates.
citation: Sherman Antitrust Act; NY Donnelly Act (GBL § 340)

q: Before closing, the cooperating broker's office asks the selling salesperson where to send her share of the commission. What is the proper answer?
options: Pay me directly, since my license permits it
Pay me directly if my broker consents in writing
Pay my brokerage; I can be paid only through my broker
Pay the seller's attorney, who will forward it to me
explanation: A salesperson may receive compensation only from her own associated broker. The cooperating firm pays her brokerage, which then pays her under their split. Her broker's consent does not allow direct payment.
